subtitulo: Ali Pasha of Ioannina, privatized sovereignty, and why 1821 was possible (1788 – 1822)

coda.heading: Coda for the journey: what to look for
intro: From Corfu, look toward the mainland. Those mountains are Ali's Epirus. If you have a free day, the ferry to Igoumenitsa crosses in a little over an hour, and from there it is another hour and a half to Ioannina: the lake, the kastro, the island in the lake where Ali was finally cut down, and the museum. It is the only way to grasp physically why the Ionian Islands were for centuries the maritime counterpart to a continental power that never touched them.

items.text: If you don't cross over, do it mentally every time you see the mainland coast. The relationship between island and mainland — trade, refugees, smuggling, mutual dependence and mistrust — is the enduring pattern of this geography, and it still operates: the coast you see is today the European Union's external border with Albania, with everything that implies for the transit of people and goods.

The city took in mainlanders fleeing Ali, just as it took in refugees from Constantinople in 1456, and just as it would take in the displaced of the twentieth century's wars. It is an island made of people who arrived escaping something, and that is probably the most productive ethnographic key you can carry with you.

sections.heading: A state within the empire, in full view of Corfu
paragraphs: From the Esplanade of Corfu you can see, across the channel, the mountains of Epirus. Between 1788 and 1822, that territory — from the Adriatic to Thessaly, with its capital at Ioannina — was ruled by Ali Pasha of Tepelena, a Muslim Albanian born around 1740, the son of a bandit chief, who began as a highway robber, obtained Ottoman offices, and ended up administering a domain of nearly one hundred thousand square kilometers with his own army, his own foreign policy, his own customs service, and a court that received ambassadors.

Formally he was a governor appointed by the sultan. Materially he was a sovereign. He negotiated directly with Napoleon and with the British, signed treaties, kept agents in Venice and Malta, funded public works, monopolized trade in his territories, and in 1809 hosted Byron, who left behind a portrait of him both fascinated and horrified: exquisite courtesy, refined hospitality, and a systematic cruelty of which legends circulated across Europe.

Ali Pasha is not an exotic curiosity. He is the clearest manifestation of a structural process: the PRIVATIZATION OF SOVEREIGNTY within an empire whose center could no longer sustain direct control. Between 1750 and 1820, local powers of this type sprang up across the whole Ottoman periphery — the so-called ayan, provincial notables with troops of their own —: Mehmet Ali in Egypt, Pazvantoglu in Vidin, the Mamluks in Baghdad. The sultan in effect legalized that situation in the so-called Deed of Alliance of 1808, a document that recognized rights for provincial notables against the throne and that is often compared to an Ottoman Magna Carta. The empire was turning into a federation of warlords who paid tribute.

sections.heading: How to govern a territory without institutions
paragraphs: Ali's technique is a textbook case of PATRIMONIALISM in the strict Weberian sense: there is no distinction between the ruler's patrimony and the public treasury, offices are personal, revocable grants, the administration consists of his sons and his clients, and loyalty is bought or extracted. He installed one son as pasha of the Morea and another at Lepanto. He accumulated agrarian estates — çiftliks — in enormous quantities, becoming the largest landowner in the region. And he practiced a policy of resettlement and selective destruction of communities that resisted him.

The most remembered episode is the war against the Souliotes, from 1803 to its final outcome: Christian mountain communities with clan organization that resisted for years and were finally expelled. Greek tradition preserves the scene of the women of Souli who, according to the story, danced on the edge of the Zalongo cliff and threw themselves off with their children rather than be captured. The scene is probably a later construction; the monument has existed since 1961 and the dance is taught in schools. Its historicity matters less than its function: the episode turned a war between an Albanian pasha and a handful of mountain clans into an act of Greek national martyrology.

And yet here is the nuance that dismantles the simplification: Ali Pasha employed Greeks in his administration, funded Greek schools in Ioannina — which was one of the great centers of the neo-Greek Enlightenment, with an academy that trained a good part of the period's intellectuals —, spoke Greek at his court, and used Christian armatoloi as troops. His state was not "Turks" oppressing "Greeks": it was a patrimonial structure that recruited by loyalty, not by religion. The ethnic reading of the conflict is a later projection, and to test it from Corfu, looking at those mountains, is a useful exercise against retrospective nationalism.

sections.heading: The condition of possibility for 1821
paragraphs: In 1820, Sultan Mahmud II — intent on recentralizing the empire — declared Ali Pasha a rebel and sent a large army against him. The campaign lasted more than a year and absorbed the Ottoman forces available in the western Balkans. Ali held out entrenched in Ioannina and was finally killed in January 1822; his head was sent to Istanbul.

The Greek revolution broke out in March 1821, in the middle of that siege. It is no coincidence: THE EMPIRE WAS BUSY DESTROYING ITS OWN VICEROY when the Peloponnese rose up, and it had no troops to put it down in the critical months. What is more, the Souliote and Albanian fighters discharged by the war swelled the revolutionary ranks, and part of Epirus's arsenal and military experience ended up on the Greek side.

The methodological lesson is important, and it applies to any analysis of revolutionary conjunctures: uprisings succeed not when oppression is at its peak but when the state's REPRESSIVE CAPACITY is temporarily compromised. It is the classic thesis of the historical sociology of revolutions, and this case illustrates it with unusual clarity. Apply it to Peru as well: the independence of 1821 was possible because Spain had been bled dry by the Napoleonic invasion and the constitutional crisis, not because criollo discontent had reached some new boiling point. And the rebellion of Túpac Amaru II in 1780, with indigenous discontent probably greater still, failed precisely because the colonial apparatus was intact and could concentrate its forces.

sections.heading: The strongman as a form of state: Ali Pasha and the gamonal
paragraphs: The figure of Ali Pasha makes it possible to pose with precision a problem that runs through the following two centuries in Greece and in Peru: what happens when effective power over a territory rests in one man and his network, rather than in an institution.

Nineteenth-century Peru was, in essence, a century of caudillos: between 1821 and 1845 the country had dozens of governments and a succession of military chiefs — Gamarra, Santa Cruz, Salaverry, Orbegoso, Castilla — whose power derived from personal command of troops and regional clienteles, not from office. And in the highlands, well into the twentieth century, the GAMONAL was exactly what Ali had been in Epirus on a larger scale: landowner, de facto judge, employer, moneylender, electoral authority, and armed force, with the national state present only as a signature on paper. Mariátegui put it bluntly: gamonalismo voids every law and every ordinance that stands against it, because the state does not reach where he commands.

Greece carried its own version forward. The military chiefs of the revolution and the regional notables we examined in entrega 10 did not disappear with independence: they became the kingdom's first politicians, and the assassination of Kapodistrias in 1831 at the hands of the Mavromichalis family — a Maniot clan — was precisely the result of trying to bring them under state control. The decisive difference between the two countries lies in the long run: Greece ended up absorbing those local powers into a centralized state apparatus that turned them into clientelist networks dependent on the budget, while Peru took much longer and in some regions never completed the process. Absorbing the caudillo into the state produces clientelism; failing to absorb him produces the absence of the state. Neither is good news, but the first is a form of integration and the second is not.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world and the Ionians as counterpart
paragraphs: While Ali Pasha was building his domain, the Ionian Islands — visible across the channel — passed from Venice to France, to the Septinsular Republic, back to France, and finally to the British protectorate in 1815, as we saw in entrega 12. Ali negotiated with all of them in turn: he wanted Parga and other mainland-coast strongholds the islands controlled, and obtained them in 1819 when the British ceded them, triggering the exodus of their population to Corfu. That episode — a European power handing over a Christian city to a pasha in exchange for regional stability — outraged philhellenic opinion in Europe, and is a useful reminder that governments' philhellenism was far more flexible than that of the poets.

Elsewhere in the world, these are the years of the Napoleonic Wars and their liquidation at the Congress of Vienna in 1815, of the Restoration system designed by Metternich to smother every revolution, and of the Spanish American independences that system failed to prevent. Greece would rise in 1821 against the very logic of the Vienna order, which regarded the Greek insurgents as the rebellious subjects of a legitimate sovereign. That the powers eventually intervened in Greece's favor in 1827 owes nothing to a change of principle, but to the calculation that a small Greece under European tutelage was preferable to an independent Greece under Russian influence.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026 and the close of Block II
paragraphs: Ali Pasha's contemporary resonance is twofold. On one hand, Ioannina is today a Greek university city, and its castle, the kastro, with the Aslan Pasha Mosque and the pasha's tomb, is a tourist destination: the tyrant figure has become a heritage attraction, with the discomfort that entails when schools still teach Zalongo. On the other, and more importantly, the type of power Ali embodied — armed territorial control, its own extractive economy, direct negotiation with external powers, indifference to the law of the nominal state — is not a premodern residue. It is a fully contemporary form of political organization, and it describes with precision what happens today across wide stretches of the Peruvian Amazon with illegal mining and the coca economy, where there is effective authority, de facto taxation, organized violence, and the absence of the state. Political sociology calls these criminal governance orders, and the best way to understand them is not as an anomaly but as the normal way a vacuum of sovereignty gets filled.

With this, Block II comes to a close. Let me recap the thread of the six entregas, because Block III will assume it as known. The Ottoman Empire governed by administering religious difference and delegating to the institutions of the dominated, which preserved Greek identity while integrating it into the apparatus of extraction (9). The four centuries were not an empty parenthesis: there was dense local autonomy, agrarian deterioration during imperial decline, and a culture of honor wherever the state did not reach (10). The Phanariot intermediary elite made the system possible, produced the cultural infrastructure of nationalism, and by breaking, brought about the destruction of mediation itself (11). A bourgeoisie formed outside the territory, under a foreign flag, financed the nation and retains its fiscal privilege to this day (12). A literate minority invented the classical ancestor and lost Rigas's multiethnic project, with consequences that would come due in 1922 (13). And the empire arrived at 1821 so decentralized that it could not suppress the revolution because it was busy destroying its own warlord (14).
Block III examines what was built out of all that: a national state with borders drawn by others, an imported king, a debt older than the state itself, and less than a third of Greeks inside it.
